A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PPRM research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, table, references, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-classification and LLM monitoring experiments in Section 5, plus MedGemma and wireless-channel experiments in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds empirical false-alarm evaluation, stationary simulations, sensitivity analyses, and intermittent-label experiments.

M1.justification: The main PPRM estimator and adaptive weighting procedure remain, but Appendix D.4 adds a hybrid procedure combining PPRM on labeled rounds with an unsupervised proxy bound on unlabeled rounds. Unlike v1's requirement for labels at every round, this extension supports intermittent labels and introduces a substantive additional monitoring component.

E1.justification: The original image, QA, medical-domain, and wireless coverage is retained. v2 substantially expands evaluated conditions through stationary Bernoulli simulations, a no-shift LLM scenario, abrupt shifts in image and QA tasks, and intermittent-label image streams (Appendices A.4 and D). These are new scenarios rather than new named benchmarks.

E2.justification: The established SRM, URM, and ideal-PPRM comparators remain in the matched original experiments. Figure 12 expands image comparisons to include fixed-weight PPRM alongside adaptive PPRM, SRM, and ideal PPRM; v1's explicit fixed-versus-adaptive comparison was confined to the LLM experiment in Table 1.

E3.justification: Original defaults remain, including one labeled and 15 unlabeled samples per round and window length 60. Added experiments introduce a null-crossing evaluation with target delta_T = 0.15, stationary simulation with risk 0.5 and threshold 0.42, window-length and controlled predictor-accuracy sweeps, and label periods k = 1, 2, 3, 4. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's predictor comparisons, adaptive-weight ablation, and non-monotonic shifts, v2 adds empirical false-alarm checks, theoretical-delay validation, window sensitivity, abrupt-shift tests, controlled poor-predictor analyses, weighting and variance diagnostics, and intermittent-label robustness tests (Figures 5, 6, and 10–14).

E5.justification: Section 5 changes the stated figure uncertainty summary from the full range across runs to mean plus or minus one standard deviation, called confidence intervals. v2 also describes averaging cumulative alarm indicators across independent null trials. Neither version specifies numerical run or seed counts, so an increase in repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1's values remain unchanged, including 519.08 versus 498.31 for fixed versus adaptive PPRM with Qwen2-VL-7B. Substantial new results include false-alarm curves below 0.15, simulated mean detection times of 91.74 for PPRM versus 231.96 for SRM in Figure 6, and window, predictor-quality, abrupt-shift, and intermittent-label findings. These are additional results, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds stationary Bernoulli assumptions, estimator-variance and normalized detection-time derivations, and Proposition A.1's approximate delay-improvement condition. Appendix D.4 adds the intermittent-label risk decomposition and hybrid lower bound. Equations 26 and 38 also correct the covariance to pair true and surrogate losses on the same labeled input.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims of semi-supervised PPRM, unbiased risk estimation, anytime-valid error control, adaptive weighting, and faster harmful-shift detection across three application areas. Splitting adaptive weighting into its own contribution bullet and replacing false-alarm terminology with type-I error do not change those claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive qualifications: variance reduction must offset the normalization penalty for faster detection; fixed weighting can underperform SRM with poor predictors; and window length trades responsiveness to abrupt changes against stability under gradual changes. Appendix D also explains interpolation toward unsupervised monitoring and discusses computational-cost tradeoffs.

D1.justification: Appendix D.5 adds qualitative implementation guidance about lightweight coefficient estimation and online, offline, or self-predictor deployment, without runtime measurements. Conversely, Figure 3's caption no longer identifies Qwen2-VL-7B as its imputation model. This removes a documented configuration detail without establishing that the model actually changed.

R1.justification: v2 adds Howard et al. (2020) to support the linear-boundary delay analysis and sharpens the distinction between persistent degradation monitoring and instantaneous-risk violations. Most other reference changes concern author names or publication metadata for already-cited works, rather than new research positioning.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order largely remain. v2 makes localized grammatical and terminology corrections, clarifies notation, reorganizes the contribution bullets, adds acknowledgements, and organizes new material into Appendices A.4 and D. The retained prose is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial diagnostic visualizations in Figures 5, 6, and 10–14 and revises existing axes, legends, label orientation, captions, and panel grouping. The earlier supplementary Figures 5–7 are retained as Figures 7–9; their renumbering is not an addition or removal. Table 1 retains its structure.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence explaining when faster detection is credible: it checks false alarms, tests poor predictors and monitoring-window choices, and derives an explicit variance-versus-normalization tradeoff. These additions address important gaps in v1's largely benchmark-based support and expose failure conditions rather than merely adding favorable scores. The gains outweigh the limited documentation regression in Figure 3 and imprecise confidence-interval terminology. The delay analysis remains approximate, and experimental repetition counts remain unspecified.
